books.title: World History
books.subtitle: From the first farmers to the global age — the human story taught as one connected arc
books.level: Secondary school world history → university survey + UPSC/AP exam readiness
books.description: The world’s story told as one arc rather than a parade of nations. The historian’s craft first — sources, periodisation, the BC/CE convention, the difference between a document and a ruin; then the pre-1200 world (the Neolithic revolution, the first cities of Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus and China, the classical Mediterranean, the Silk Roads); the early-modern crossings (the Ottoman-Safavid-Mughal-Ming-Qing land empires, the Indian Ocean and trans-Saharan exchange networks, the European voyages and the Columbian exchange); the Atlantic revolutions (the Enlightenment, America, France, Haiti, Latin America); the industrial revolution and capitalism’s forms; nationalism and the age of imperialism 1870-1914; the world wars with the Russian Revolution, fascism and the Holocaust; the Cold War, decolonisation and the redrawal of national boundaries; and globalisation with the political philosophies — communism, capitalism, socialism — the UPSC register prices. Cross-references Indian History (the colonial and imperial bridge where the two arcs meet) and hands off to Political Science (the nation-state’s ideas) and to the reader’s own present.

chapters.title: The Historian’s Craft
chapters.summary: How history is actually written: primary against secondary sources, the literary against the archaeological register, external and internal criticism of a document, the archaeologist’s sherd against the court chronicle; periodisation as a CONVENTION (the ancient/medieval/modern triad interrogated, not assumed) and the BC/BCE-CE dating census; and the map of this book’s arc stated honestly — why world history is taught as one story and what that choice costs.
planned: Chapter XIII. The Sources of Plato's Opinions

chapters.title: The World Before 1200
chapters.summary: The long runway: the Palaeolithic scatter and the Neolithic revolution (agriculture as the first technology of consequence); the first cities — Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus civilisation, Shang China; the classical age of Greece and Rome with its political inventions; the great empires of land and their collapse; the Silk Roads and the Buddhist-Christian-Islamic travels of religion; the world as the 1200 starting line found it — Song China, the Abbasid twilight, feudal Europe, the African kingdoms and the Americas apart.
planned: The Classical World: Greece and Rome
The Silk Roads and the Medieval World
The World in 1200: the Starting Line

Agriculture - major crops and cropping patterns, irrigation systems, storage, transport and marketing of agricultural produce, e-technology in the aid of farmers; direct and indirect farm subsidies and minimum support prices; Public Distribution System and food security; food processing and related
Preface to the First Edition (signed M. Laxmikanth)

chapters.title: Land-Based Empires
chapters.summary: The early-modern land powers: the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal gunpowder empires with their legitimation craft (the devshirme, the Safavid Shi’a state, Mughal syncretism); Ming-Qing China’s tribute system and the examination state; the Aztec and Inca empires of the Americas; the pastoral-nomadic and forest frontiers; and the fiscal-military logic that let these empires rule vast agrarian interiors before oceanic power rearranged the world.
planned: Ming-Qing China and the Tribute World
About the Civil Services Examination — A. Preliminary Examination / B. Main Examination (Qualifying Papers: Paper A, Paper B)

chapters.title: Networks of Exchange
chapters.summary: The connective tissue of the pre-1500 world: the Indian Ocean monsoon system with its Gujarati and Swahili merchants; the trans-Saharan caravan routes and Mansa Musa’s gold; the Silk Roads’ goods, technologies and diseases; the diasporas of traders and the spread of religion along the routes; and the growing comparison — the land routes against the sea routes that were about to win.
planned: The Land and Sea Route Comparison

chapters.title: Transoceanic Interconnections
chapters.summary: The European voyages: the Portuguese around Africa, Columbus west, Magellan’s circumnavigation, the trading-post empire that followed; the Columbian exchange as the world’s biggest biological event (crops, animals, diseases and their demographic earthquakes); the Atlantic system’s beginning with the plantation complex and the rise of the slave trade; and the first global silver economy threading Mexico to Ming China.

chapters.title: The Atlantic Revolutions
chapters.summary: The Enlightenment’s ideas and their combustions: the American revolution and its constitutional invention; the French Revolution from the Estates to the Terror, Napoleon and its impact; the Haitian revolution as the only successful slave revolt; the Latin American independence wars under Bolivar and San Martin; the abolition movement’s first wave; and the revolutions’ global echoes — the idea that sovereignty lives in the people crosses the world.
planned: The Abolition Wave and the Echoes

chapters.title: Industry and Capital
chapters.summary: The industrial revolution: why Britain first (coal, colonies, capital, the patent culture), the factory system, the steam and steel engines, the railway and telegraph shrinking distance; capitalism’s forms and the workers’ world it made (the condition-of-England question, the new cities, the public-health disasters and reforms); socialism as the century’s answer; and the industrial-military engine that armed the coming imperial scramble — the GS1 register’s political-philosophies line begins here.
planned: The Factory World and Its Cities
Capitalism, Socialism and the Century’s Debate

chapters.title: Nationalism and Imperialism
chapters.summary: The nation-state system: nationalism’s theory and its engines (print, schools, language standardisation), the unifications of Italy and Germany, the multi-national empires’ dilemma; the age of imperialism 1870-1914 — the Scramble for Africa at Berlin’s table, the Raj’s consolidation, China’s century of humiliation, Japan’s Meiji exception; the colonised world’s responses from the Brahmo to the Boxer; and the system’s tension accumulating toward 1914.
planned: The Scramble and the Age of Imperialism
Globalisation - responses from developed and developing societies

chapters.title: The World Wars
chapters.summary: The thirty years’ crisis: the Great War’s causes, course and peace treaties with Wilson’s hope against the mandates; the Russian Revolution from February to October, the civil war and the Soviet experiment; the interwar world — the Depression, fascism and Nazism explained honestly, the League’s failure; the Second World War’s theatres, the Holocaust as its own chapter of grief, the resistance movements, and the war’s end at Hiroshima — the UPSC register’s ’world wars’ line carried in full.
planned: The Great War and Its Peace
Fascism, Nazism and the Interwar World
The Second World War: Theatres and the Holocaust
Chapter VI. Saint Benedict and Gregory the Great
Chapter XV. The Eclipse of the Papacy

chapters.title: The Cold War and Decolonisation
chapters.summary: The post-1945 order: the UN’s founding and the Security Council’s arithmetic; the Cold War’s logic, its crises (Berlin, Korea, Cuba, Vietnam) and its arms race; decolonisation across Asia and Africa with the partition’s price, the Bandung spirit and the non-aligned; the redrawal of national boundaries as empires dissolved; the Middle East’s wars and oil; and the Soviet collapse ending the bipolar era — GS1’s decolonisation register in full.
planned: The UN and the Postwar Order
The Cold War’s Crises and Races
Global Conflict, the Cold War and Decolonization

chapters.title: Globalisation and the Doorstep
chapters.summary: The world since 1991: globalisation’s dimensions (trade, capital, people, data) and its discontents; the political philosophies’ final accounting — communism’s variants, capitalism’s forms, social democracy’s third way, their forms and effects on society (the GS1 line closed); the climate agenda and the global institutions; the multipolar present with its rising powers; and the doorstep — to Indian History’s post-independence arc (the two books meet at 1947’s bridge), and to International Relations and Political Science for the order’s theory.
planned: The Doorstep: India’s Arc and the Order’s Theory

books.title: Indian History
books.subtitle: The subcontinent’s whole arc — stone age to republic — in one connected chronicle
books.level: Secondary school Indian history → university survey + UPSC/state-PSC exam readiness
books.description: India’s past as one national chronicle across the folded three periods. The sources’ craft first (archaeological, literary and foreign accounts, the periodisation debate); the prehistoric and Harappan foundations; the Vedic world and the second urbanisation with Buddhism and Jainism; the Mahajanapadas to the Mauryan empire (Ashoka’s dhamma, the Arthashastra, Megasthenes) and the post-Mauryan worlds through the Guptas and Harsha; the early-medieval south (the Chola triad’s age, the southeast-Asian reach); the Delhi Sultanate’s five dynasties with the Vijayanagar-Bahmani south; the Mughal empire’s establishment, administration and culture and its decline; the eighteenth century’s regional powers and the European penetration (Plassey and Buxar); colonial rule, the reform movements and the 1857 revolt; the freedom struggle’s full arc from the Moderates to Gandhi’s mass movements, the revolutionaries and the INA, partition and independence; post-independence consolidation, reorganisation and the republic’s decades; and the art-and-culture thread that runs the whole length. Cross-references World History (the imperial bridge) and hands off to Art History (the object register), Archaeology (the material record) and Political Science (the Constitution’s history).

chapters.title: The Sources and the Periodisation
chapters.summary: India’s history’s evidence: the archaeological register (sites, inscriptions, coins, monuments), the literary register (the Vedas to the medieval chronicles, their dating problems), the foreign accounts (Megasthenes, Fa-Hien, Hiuen Tsang, Al-Biruni and the Europeans); the periodisation debate — the ancient/medieval/modern triad as a colonial-era convention interrogated honestly against the indigenist alternatives; and the map of this book’s twelve-chapter arc.
planned: Chapter III. Three Doctors of the Church
Chapter V. The Fifth and Sixth Centuries

chapters.title: Prehistoric and Harappan India
chapters.summary: The Palaeolithic stations of the subcontinent (the Sohan and Madras industries), the Mesolithic microliths and the Neolithic-chalcolithic villages of the Deccan and the Ganga valley; the Harappan civilisation in full — town planning (the grid, the great bath, the drainage), society and economy (the seals, the weights, the trade with Mesopotamia), the major sites’ census, the script’s undeciphered honesty, and the decline’s competing theories (climate, the river’s shift, the ’Aryan’ question retired carefully).
planned: The Harappan Town and Its Craft

Paper-II 1. Evolution of the Indian Culture and Civilization (prehistoric and protohistoric cultures; pre-Harappan, Harappan and post-Harappan; palaeo-anthropological evidences from India; ethno-archaeology in India)

chapters.title: The Vedic World and the Second Urbanisation
chapters.summary: The Vedic corpus as social evidence — the Rigveda’s pastoral world, the later Vedic’s agrarian turn, the varna system’s elaboration, the Upanishadic turn of thought; the sixth-century BCE’s second urbanisation (the Ganga cities, iron, coinage) and its two great dissents — Mahavira’s Jainism and the Buddha’s path with their sanghas and the Pali canon; and the sixteen Mahajanapadas’ politics ending at the Nandas.
planned: Preface to the Sixth Edition (continued — signed M. Laxmikanth)

chapters.title: From the Mauryas to the Guptas
chapters.summary: The Mauryan empire: Chandragupta and Kautilya’s Arthashastra, Ashoka’s inscriptions and dhamma, the administration-economy-art census and Megasthenes’ account; the post-Mauryan arrivals — the Indo-Greeks, the Shakas, the Kushanas and the Satavahanas with the three art schools (Gandhara, Mathura, Amaravati); the imperial Guptas’ golden-age question priced honestly (administration, the sciences, the arts); and Harsha’s Kanauj as the ancient arc’s close.
planned: The Mauryan State and Ashoka’s Dhamma
The Post-Mauryan World and the Art Schools
The Guptas and the Golden-Age Question

chapters.title: The Early Medieval South
chapters.summary: The peninsular powers the northern chronicles skip: the Age of the Three Empires (800-1000) — the Rashtrakutas, the Pratiharas and the Palas in their tripartite struggle; the Cholas’ state (the village assemblies’ uttaramerur evidence, the navy, the Rajendra raids), the temple as the era’s economic and cultural engine; the southeast-Asian cultural reach (the Pallava-Chola hands in the Khmer and Srivijaya worlds); and the regional kingdoms’ census across the peninsula.
planned: The Chola State and Its Assemblies

chapters.title: The Delhi Sultanate
chapters.summary: The five dynasties — the Mamluks, the Khaljis, the Tughlaqs, the Sayyids and the Lodis — with their character (the market reforms and the capital experiments priced as both bold and failed); the Sultanate’s administration (iqta, the ministries), its economy and its society; the Mongol containment; the Sultanate’s architecture (the arch and the dome arrive — the Qutb, the Lodi tombs); and the peninsular answer — Vijayanagar and the Bahmanis’ long duel.

chapters.title: The Mughal Empire
chapters.summary: Babur to Aurangzeb as one arc: the establishment (Panipat, the Humayun interregnum, Sher Shah’s administration), Akbar’s synthesis (the sulah-i-kul, the mansabdari engine, the Rajput alliance), Jahangir and Shah Jahan’s culture, Aurangzeb’s expansion and its costs; the empire’s institutions priced (the jagir crisis honestly); the art-and-architecture register (the Fatehpur Sikri, the Taj, the atelier) with the depth handed to Art History; the Rajputs and the Marathas’ rise (Shivaji’s swarajya); and the decline’s historiography.
planned: The Marathas and the Decline’s Historiography

chapters.title: The Eighteenth Century
chapters.summary: The post-Mughal regional order — the successor states (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad, the Sikhs, the Jats, the Rohillas) and the eighteenth-century debate (was it a ’dark age’? no — priced against the scholarship); the European companies’ arrival as traders; the Carnatic wars; Plassey and Buxar as the conquest’s hinge; the British consolidation’s policies and their economic, administrative and socio-cultural impact (the drain priced honestly) — the bridge where this book and World History’s imperial arc meet.
planned: The Carnatic Wars and the Companies

chapters.title: Colonial Rule and the Response
chapters.summary: The colonial state’s construction: the acts from 1773 to 1858 and the Crown’s Raj (the Political Science book owns the constitutional history’s analytical register); the socio-religious reform movements (Raja Rammohan Roy, the Brahmo Samaj, the Arya Samaj, the Aligarh movement, the Singh Sabha — the reform-and-revival distinction); the deindustrialisation and the railways’ double face; and the 1857 revolt in full — causes, leaders, nature, suppression, consequences (the GS1 line carried verbatim in spirit).
planned: The Acts and the Raj’s Construction
The Reform and the Revival Movements
The Rise of Indian Nationalism and the Moderates
The Gandhian Phase and Mass Movements
The Constitution, Partition and Integration of States

Pages 3–32: body text of that same history book (Chapter 1: The Revolt of 1857 — Economic Causes, Political Causes, Administrative Causes, Socio-Religious Causes, Influence of Outside Events, Discontent Among Sepoys, Beginning and Spread, Storm Centres and Leaders of the Revolt, Suppression of

chapters.title: The Freedom Struggle
chapters.summary: The national movement’s whole arc as the GS1 register demands: the growth of nationalism (the unification’s engines — railways, press, education), the Moderates’ era, the Swadeshi and the Surat split, the revolutionary activities, Gandhi’s arrival and the Rowlatt-Jallianwala hinge, Non-Cooperation, the Swarajists and No-Changers, the Civil Disobedience and the Salt March, the Round Tables and the Act of 1935, the provincial ministries, the Left (the CSP, the trade unions), the INA and Subhas Bose, the Quit India and the Cabinet Mission, and partition with independence — the contributors from every part of the country priced.
planned: Gandhi’s Arrival and the Mass Movements
The Left, the Revolutionaries and the INA
Modern Indian History: The Significant Events, Personalities and Issues

chapters.title: Post-Independence India
chapters.summary: The republic’s narrative decades (the analytical polity belongs to Political Science; the story lives here): partition’s aftermath and the princely states’ integration (Patel and Menon’s craft), the linguistic reorganisation, the official-language question, the Constitution’s framing and framing moments (cross-referenced), the planned economy and the Green Revolution, the wars with China and Pakistan and the nuclear turn, the non-aligned foreign policy (cross-referenced to International Relations), the Emergency, the coalition era and the LPG reforms — the GS1 ’post-independence consolidation and reorganisation’ line carried in full.
planned: The Planned Economy and the Green Revolution
The Wars and the Foreign-Policy Arc
The Emergency, Coalitions and the Reforms

chapters.title: The Culture Thread and the Doorstep
chapters.summary: The long thread that ran through every chapter — the art forms, literature and architecture from the Bhakti-Sufi worlds to the modern renaissance — gathered as one register and handed to Art History for the object-level depth and to Cultural Studies for the contemporary; the synthesis map of the whole chronicle; and the doorstep — to Political Science (the Constitution), to World History (the imperial arc this story was embedded in), and to the reader’s own family as the arc’s living continuation.
planned: The Doorstep: the Republic and Beyond
Part I. From the Renaissance to Hume

books.title: Political Science
books.subtitle: Power, ideas and the state — from political theory to the working of the Indian Constitution
books.level: Secondary school civics → university political science + UPSC/state-PSC/UGC-NET readiness
books.description: The discipline in one arc. What politics is (power, authority, legitimacy, the state’s definitions) and the approaches; the political theory core — freedom, equality, social justice, rights, citizenship, secularism, nationalism as CONTESTED concepts each with their thinkers; the ideologies — liberalism, conservatism, socialism, nationalism, feminism, ecologism, with political economy and globalisation; democracy’s models and legitimacy, elections, representation, voting behaviour; constitutions, the rule of law, executives, legislatures, judiciaries and the separation of powers; then the Indian spine: the Constitution’s making, salient features, fundamental rights and duties, the federal structure, parliament, the executive and the judiciary, elections and the RPA, constitutional bodies; parties, pressure groups, political culture and identity politics; Indian political thought (Kautilya, Gandhi, Ambedkar, Aurobindo); the comparative glance; and the world-order pointer. Cross-references International Relations (the world-order depth), Public Administration (the governance machinery) and Law and Legal Studies (the constitutional-law depth) and hands off to the Humanities shelf’s Ethics for public-values register.

chapters.title: What Is Politics?
chapters.summary: The discipline’s first question answered four ways: politics as the exercise of power (the faces-of-power debate — the second and third faces priced), as the machinery of government, as the public sphere’s deliberation, as the allocation of values (Easton); authority’s types and legitimacy’s claim; the state’s definition and its sovereignty; and the approaches’ census — normative against empirical, behavioural, institutional, the political-economy lens — with the science’s method honestly cross-referenced to the Mathematics shelf’s statistics book.
planned: Paper-I 4. Political Organization and Social Control (band, tribe, chiefdom, kingdom and state; power, authority and legitimacy; law and justice in simple societies)

chapters.title: The Concepts of Political Theory
chapters.summary: The theory core as contested concepts (the NCERT arc): freedom’s negative and positive readings (Berlin’s two concepts, Gandhi’s freedom as swaraj); equality’s kinds — formal, substantive, of opportunity against outcome; social justice from Rawls’s veil to Ambedkar’s annihilation; rights’ classifications and the rights-duties dialectic; citizenship from the polis to the diaspora; secularism’s western and Indian models; nationalism from Herder to the anti-colonial register — every concept taught as a live argument.

chapters.title: Ideologies and the Political Economy
chapters.summary: The ideologies’ register: liberalism’s classical and social-democratic wings; conservatism’s disposition; socialism from Marx through the social democrats to the actually-existing question; nationalism’s political work; feminism’s waves and the political; ecologism’s deep and shallow greens; the political economy — capitalism’s variants, the globalisation debate (the GS register’s effects-on-society lines cross-referenced to Sociology), the welfare state’s rise and crisis.

chapters.title: Democracy and Representation
chapters.summary: Democracy’s models — direct, representative, participatory, deliberative — with legitimacy’s performance crisis; the regime census (democratic, authoritarian, hybrid — the third-wave and its reversals); elections and representation’s theories (the trustee against the delegate, the mandate theory); voting behaviour’s sociological and economic models; parties and party systems (the Sartori census; India’s party system’s evolution from the Congress system to coalition to the present); and the pressure groups, movements and interests — Heywood’s register carried whole.
planned: Civil Liberties, Civil Rights and American Political Culture

chapters.title: Constitutions and Institutions
chapters.summary: The institutional core: constitutions as higher law (codified against uncodified — the Westminster against the US model), the rule of law and judicial review, judges’ role and the appointment debates; executives — presidential against parliamentary, the leadership question; legislatures’ structure, functioning, powers and privileges; the separation of powers and its checks; the comparison of the Indian constitutional scheme with other countries (the GS2 line) — the Westminster inheritance, the US bill of rights, the French laicite as three reference points.
planned: Constitutions and the Rule of Law
Foundations of American Democracy and the Branches of Government

chapters.title: The Indian Constitution
chapters.summary: The Indian text as politics: the historical underpinnings and evolution (the 1858-1947 acts compressed — the analytical register owned by Law and Legal Studies), the making (the Assembly’s craft), the salient features; the preamble’s keywords argued; the fundamental rights and duties with the DPSP’s balance; the basic-structure doctrine earned from Kesavananda; the amendments’ census; and the working of the rights in the courts — the Laxmikanth-Basu arc with the NCERT Constitution-at-Work pedagogy.
planned: The Making and the Salient Features
Rights, Duties and the Directive Principles

chapters.title: The Indian State at Work
chapters.summary: The machinery in action: the union and the states’ functions and responsibilities, the federal structure’s issues and challenges (the GS2 line — fiscal federalism’s devolution priced), the panchayati and municipal devolution; the parliament and state legislatures’ conduct of business; the executive and the judiciary’s structure and functioning; the Representation of People’s Act’s salient features; the constitutional posts and the statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies’ census.
planned: The Union Executive: President, Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
Parliament: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha and Committees
Federalism, State Governments and Local Bodies
The Election Commission and Electoral Reforms
Constitutional and Statutory Bodies: CAG to UPSC
Theories of the State - liberal, neo-liberal, Marxist, pluralist, post-colonial and feminist

chapters.title: Identity Politics in India
chapters.summary: The political culture and the identity register: the political culture-media-identity triangle (Heywood’s chapter priced for India); the caste’s political career from Mandal to the present; the communalism and secularism’s political register (cross-referenced to Sociology’s society chapters); the regionalism and the sons-of-soil; the women’s political representation and the quota debate; and the political socialisation — how Indians become political animals.
planned: Paper-II 9. History of Administration of Tribal Areas, Tribal Policies and Programmes of Tribal Development (concept of PTGs; role of NGOs; role of anthropology in tribal and rural development; contributions to the understanding of regionalism, communalism and ethnic and political movements)

chapters.title: Indian Political Thought
chapters.summary: The thought register the UPSC PSIR paper prices: Kautilya’s Arthashastra as statecraft (the mandala theory, the spy system, the danda); the Dharmashastras’ political ideas priced carefully; Gandhi’s swaraj, satyagraha and the oceanic circles; Ambedkar’s annihilation argument, the constitutional morality and the Buddha’s dhamma; Aurobindo’s integral freedom; Vivekananda, Tagore and Savarkar as the modern debate’s poles; and the Western canon’s Indian dialogues — the comparative thought register.
planned: Indian Political Thought - Dharamshastra, Arthashastra and Buddhist traditions; Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Sri Aurobindo, M. K. Gandhi, B. R. Ambedkar, M. N. Roy

chapters.title: The World Order and the Doorstep
chapters.summary: The global register named and handed off: multilevel politics (the EU as the case), security’s domestic-international blur, world order and global governance — Heywood’s final chapters are the POINTER (the depth is International Relations’ whole book); the public policy and bureaucracy chapter as the POINTER to Public Administration; and the doorstep — to the comparative politics’ world (the AP US Government units as one reference), to International Relations for the inter-state order, and to the reader’s own political judgement.
planned: Current Affairs, including General Knowledge (national and international current affairs; political events; global environment; sports; awards and personalities; technology and science; cultural events; Indian business environment)

books.title: International Relations
books.subtitle: Anarchy and its institutions — the theory and practice of the inter-state world
books.level: Secondary school civics → university IR + UPSC (PSIR paper 2, GS-II lines) readiness
books.description: The inter-state world as its own discipline. The field’s birth (the Great War’s shock, the 1919 chairs) and its levels of analysis; the theories in full — realism classical and neo-, liberalism and the democratic peace, the English School, constructivism, Marxism and the critical theories, feminism, the post-positivist turn; war and security (the causes of war, the security dilemma, terrorism and WMD, collective security); the international history register (the modern order’s rise, the thirty-years crisis, the cold war — the NCERT Contemporary World Politics arc); international law and organisation (the UN system, the special agencies, the regional bodies, the NGOs); the global political economy (trade, finance, the WTO-IMF-World Bank trio, development’s regime); the environment and the human-security agenda; India and the world (the foreign policy’s evolution, the neighbourhood, the groupings, the diaspora — the GS2 lines 17-20 in full); the world order’s change; and the doorstep. Cross-references Political Science (the theory’s domestic twin) and World History (the order’s past) and hands off to the reader’s newsfeed.

chapters.title: The Discipline of IR
chapters.summary: The field’s own story: international relations born as a discipline from the First World War’s rubble (the 1919 Aberystwyth chair, the idealist-first age priced honestly); the core problem — anarchy (no world government, the self-help world) with the Westphalian myth interrogated (1648’s treaty read against its historiography); sovereignty’s meanings; and the levels of analysis (the individual, the state, the system — Waltz’s three images) as the book’s analytic spine.
planned: The Birth From the Great War
Federalism - constitutional provisions; changing nature of centre-state relations; integrationist tendencies and regional aspirations; inter-state disputes
Approaches to the Study of International Relations - idealist, realist, Marxist, functionalist and systems theory
Regionalisation of World Politics - EU, ASEAN, APEC, SAARC, NAFTA

chapters.title: The Theories of IR
chapters.summary: The theoretical register in full: realism from Thucydides and Machiavelli through Morgenthau to neo-realism (Waltz’s structure) and the offensive-defensive debate; liberalism — the Kantian tripod, interdependence, the democratic peace; the English School’s international society; constructivism’s Wendtian turn (anarchy is what states make of it); the radical family — Marxism, dependency, world-systems; feminism and gender in IR; the post-positivist and critical turn — every theory taught with its counter.
planned: The Radical Family and the Critical Turn

chapters.title: War and Security
chapters.summary: Security’s register: war’s causes priced (the levels applied — Thucydides’ fear-honour-interest to the bargaining model); the security dilemma and the offence-defence balance; deterrence’s logic and its nuclear age (the stability-instability paradox named); terrorism and the WMD proliferation; collective security’s idea and its record (the League’s failure priced); and the changing security concept — the Buzan widening from state to human (the NCERT security chapter’s arc).

chapters.title: The International History Register
chapters.summary: The order’s past told as IR (the narrative depth owned by World History, the interstate logic here): the modern international order’s rise from the European concert; the thirty-years crisis 1919-1949 (Versailles, the League, the appeasement); the cold war’s structure (the containment, the crises, the détente and the ending — the NCERT cold-war chapters as the spine); the post-cold-war unipolar moment; and the present multipolar question — each era read through the theories of chapter two.
planned: The Concert to the Thirty-Years Crisis

chapters.title: International Law and Organisation
chapters.summary: The legal-institutional register: international law’s sources and its enforcement problem (the anarchy’s law); the treaties’ life and the states’ consent; the UN system in full — the Charter’s structure, the Security Council’s arithmetic and the veto, the Assembly, the Secretary-General’s political role, the peacekeeping’s record, the reform debate; the special agencies’ census (the WHO, the ILO, the UNICEF family); the regional organisations (the EU’s sui generis, the ASEAN, the African Union); and the NGOs and the global civil society — the GS2 ’international institutions, agencies and fora — their structure and mandate’ line carried in full.
planned: The NGOs and the Global Civil Society

Security - linkages between development and spread of extremism; role of external state and non-state actors in internal security challenges; communication networks, media and social networking sites in internal security, basics of cyber security; money-laundering and its prevention; border
United Nations - envisaged role and actual record; specialised UN agencies; need for UN reforms

chapters.title: The Global Political Economy
chapters.summary: IPE’s register: trade’s regimes from the GATT to the WTO (the dispute settlement priced); finance’s order — the Bretton Woods system, its collapse, the IMF and the World Bank’s roles and their critiques; the global production’s chains and the South’s development question (the dependency register revisited); the sanctions’ weapon; and the economic statecraft’s present (the weaponised interdependence named) — the economic THEORY is cross-referenced to the Economics shelf’s future books, this book owns the political reading.
planned: Trade: From GATT to the WTO
The Sanctions and the Weaponised Interdependence
Evolution of the International Economic System - from Brettonwoods to WTO; socialist economies and the CMEA; Third World demand for a new international economic order
India and the Global South - relations with Africa and Latin America; leadership role in NIEO and WTO negotiations

chapters.title: The Environment and Human Security
